newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech far-right attacks declaration with Germany.
newsitem.headline: Czech far-right attacks declaration with Germany.

text.p: Far-right Czech Republicans told parliament on Tuesday that a declaration aimed at closing the book on World War Two would again lead to German domination.

With political tempers rising following a media leak of the declaration, parliamentary chairman Milos Zeman also demanded the right of the chamber to amend the text, which has yet to be signed by the Czech and German governments.

Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec promised both countries' parliaments would get the chance to debate the declaration in February but said Chancellor Helmut Kohl would probably visit Prague in the second half of January to sign it.
The declaration, in which Bonn and Prague apologise to each other for brutality or excesses during and after the Nazi occupation, has long stirred controversy in Germany.

In the Czech Republic, a fragile truce between the centre-right coalition government and the centre-left Social Democrats has largely kept the issue out of mainstream politics, although the Republicans and Communists have frequently raised the spectre of German dominance.
The Republicans, who won nine percent of the vote in lower house elections last June, led the charge on Tuesday.
Chairman Miroslav Sladek told parliament that the declaration would mean a return of Sudetens, the German minority expelled after the war for collaboration with the Nazis.

His deputy Jan Vik described the declaration, which is expected to be initialled later this month, as "a great national tragedy and another step towards the future and total control of the Czech Republic by German Federal Republic".
Vik used the name for the former West Germany used by the Communists during the Cold War which implicitly questions its legitimacy, rather than its formal title of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Vik also criticised a joint Czech-German fund proposed in the declaration for not explicitly being earmarked for Czech victims of Nazism alone. The little-reformed Communists echoed the Republicans' comments.

Parliamentary chairman Milos Zeman, who also leads the opposition Social Democrats, did not criticise the declaration but demanded a say for deputies. Zeman declined detailed comment until the declaration, obtained by some media on Monday, had been formally presented to parliament.
Zeman, although in opposition, has been involved throughout much of the two years taken to negotiate the document.

Mainstream Czech parties had largely kept the issue out of domestic politics, hoping to resolve Czech-German mistrust it would not crop up in negotiations for Czech entry to NATO and the European Union.
But Zeman, a personal rival of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, has all along stressed that parliament must have its say.
Diplomats say that Prague is keen to keep any parliamentary amendment to a brief appendix.

This follows an incident in 1992 in which the German parliament added text to a previous Czech-German treaty saying explicitly that the issue of property confiscated from Sudeten Germans remained unsettled.
Zieleniec, who is expected to initial the declaration on December 20 with his German counterpart Klaus Kinkel, said parliament would have its say.

"It's important that the parliaments of the Czech Republic and Germany discuss the document in parallel ... Provisionally we expect that the session which is due to start at the beginning of February should discuss the text," he said.

But he emphasised that the two governments would get to work earlier. Asked when Kohl could visit Prague to sign the document with Klaus, he said: "The second part of January seems to be an appropriate time."
